articles.body: Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite into orbit within less than 60 days according to new Western intelligence assessments reported Monday, raising fears that Moscow is preparing to deploy a weapon capable of crippling thousands of satellites used by the United States and its allies. The intelligence reports emerged just four days after President Donald Trump met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a high-profile summit in Shenzhen, China, where nuclear arms control was a central topic. The three leaders issued a joint declaration affirming that nuclear war should never be fought, but stopped short of announcing binding arms-control commitments. NEXT GENERATION OPIR GEO: BUILDING AMERICA’S GATEWAY TO THE FUTURE OF SPACE-BASED MISSILE WARNING AND TRACKING On Monday, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz publicly addressed the reports, while the Kremlin dismissed the allegations. According to a joint investigation published Nov. 23 by German broadcasters WDR and NDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung, Western intelligence agencies believe Russia has assembled a satellite known as "Sputnik-S," which has reportedly been stored in the Moscow region for several years. Intelligence warnings shared among several NATO countries in early November indicated that the satellite, reportedly designed to carry a nuclear warhead, could be launched within 60 days. Germany's military Space Command reportedly assessed that a December launch was possible. The German investigation also reported that military officials had briefed senior government figures, including German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, about the threat. The reports prompted an immediate response from European leaders. Speaking alongside Rutte in Berlin on Monday, Merz described the allegations as "shocking," while noting that concerns about Russia's nuclear space ambitions were not entirely new. PUTIN LAUNCHES UKRAINE BARRAGE HOURS AFTER TRUMP MEETING AMID ALLEGED RUSSIAN MISSILE BREACH OF NATO AIRSPACE Rutte, meanwhile, stressed that NATO was continually assessing its defensive capabilities. "I can assure you, we will always make sure that we defend every inch of NATO territory," Rutte said, according to Reuters. He added that the alliance's defense planning included threats in space and said NATO had response options that were not always visible to the public. The Kremlin rejected the allegations. Russian presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov questioned the credibility of the intelligence reports, saying they contained numerous unsubstantiated claims that were "hardly worth taking seriously," according to The Moscow Times. "We haven’t seen the report. But there are so many ‘alleged’ and ‘possible’ claims in it, attributed to who knows whom, that it’s certainly hardly worth taking them seriously," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing. Russia's Embassy in Berlin separately dismissed the reporting as part of a propaganda campaign and maintained that Moscow's space activities were peaceful and consistent with international obligations. The latest warnings follow an earlier assessment by the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency , which publicly identified Russia's development of a nuclear-capable satellite in October. "Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon," the DIA stated in its 2026 Challenges to Security in Space assessment. NATO WARNS RUSSIA: 'WE WILL BREAK' FORCES, DESTROY 'ANYTHING AND EVERYTHING' IF YOU ATTACK As Fox News Digital reported on October 29, the agency warned that such a weapon could cause the rapid loss or degradation of thousands of satellites operated by governments and private companies. Unlike a conventional anti-satellite weapon targeting an individual spacecraft, a nuclear detonation in orbit could potentially disable large numbers of satellites through radiation and electromagnetic effects. The consequences could extend far beyond the military. Satellites support GPS navigation, international communications, financial transactions, weather forecasting and critical infrastructure. The threat also has implications for Ukraine, whose military relies heavily on satellite communications, including SpaceX's Starlink network, during its war with Russia. The concern was initially addressed on February 2024 when the Biden administration publicly acknowledged that Russia was developing a troubling anti-satellite capability, although officials said at the time that no such weapon had been deployed. Placing a nuclear weapon in orbit would violate the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which prohibits stationing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in space. The latest German reporting suggests the threat could be approaching a more immediate stage, but critical questions remain unanswered, including whether the satellite already carries a nuclear warhead and whether Western intelligence has independently verified the reported launch preparations. articles.title: Turkish police hunting for lioness stalking Istanbul
articles.summary: Questions being asked about big cat’s origins, with suspicion falling on the country’s growing role in animal smuggling.
articles.body:
Police and animal welfare teams have launched a hunt for a lioness reported to be prowling the outskirts of Istanbul.

City authorities closed a woodland area in the northern Sariyer district on Monday as the teams expanded a search for the big cat, which was spotted in the area the previous evening.

Turkiye’s National Parks Directorate said on Sunday that police officers in Zekeriyakoy, north of Istanbul’s European side, had reported spotting “an animal resembling a lion” on surveillance cameras.

Grainy security camera footage republished by Turkish media appeared to show what looked like a big cat prowling across a patch of open countryside.

Istanbul Governor Davut Gul’s office confirmed the information, saying that “the necessary care is being taken to capture it alive”.

The parks authority said specialist veterinarians and teams equipped with thermal imaging cameras were assisting in the search.

More than 70 personnel, supported by drones, were searching in and around the nearby Belgrade Forest, which covers 54 square kilometres (21 square miles) north of Istanbul.

Local resident Arda Koc said he saw the lioness after joining the search on Sunday evening.

“I took my car and went out for a drive hoping to see it,” he told Turkiye’s Cumhuriyet newspaper. “While I was driving, it suddenly jumped out in front of me. At first I was scared. After that, I immediately notified the gendarmerie.”

Residents have been warned of the danger, and police were stationed on roads leading into and out of the neighbourhood.

Sariyer District Mayor Mustafa Oktay Aksu noted that the lioness had not harmed chickens she passed at night, indicating she had been hand-reared. However, he warned that she should still be treated as dangerous.

Meanwhile, activists and professors have questioned how the species was brought into Turkiye.

Doganay Tolunay, a professor in the forestry department of Istanbul University-Cerrahpasa, said on X on Monday that questions that need to be asked should include “how a globally threatened species was brought into our country, how it got through customs, why those feeding it have yet to be identified” and “what will happen if the lion is caught”.

Turkiye has become a hub for the illegal trade in wild animals as traffickers exploit its air links to Africa and Asia.

In December 2024, a young gorilla was rescued after being discovered at Istanbul Airport on a flight from Nigeria to Thailand.

articles.title: Dutch transgender activist Jason Bhugwandass dies by euthanasia at 28 after years of physical and mental health struggles; Prime Minister Rob Jetten and Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema pay tribute
articles.summary: Dutch transgender activist Jason Bhugwandass, who dedicated his life to exposing alleged abuses in youth care institutions, has died by euthanasia at the
articles.body: Dutch transgender activist Jason Bhugwandass, who dedicated his life to exposing alleged abuses in youth care institutions, has died by euthanasia at the age of 28 following years of serious physical and mental health struggles. His death has prompted tributes from Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten and Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema, who remembered him for his courage and efforts to give vulnerable young people a voice.Jetten said he was deeply affected by the news, praising Bhugwandass for speaking up against mistreatment in youth care centres and standing up for people who had experienced similar treatment.“Deeply affected by the death of Jason Bhugwandass. The way he fought against abuses in youth care over the past few years deserves respect and appreciation,” the Prime Minister said. “He gave others who had been through the same things the voice he himself had so sorely missed.”He also offered his condolences to Bhugwandass' loved ones and everyone who had cared for him.Jason Bhugwandass' health struggles and final daysThe activist's death was announced through a statement shared on his Instagram account on Saturday. It said he had experienced symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) for years and had later developed a functional neurological disorder and Lance-Adams syndrome, a rare movement disorder.“The combination of these conditions reinforced each other and severely limited him in his daily life,” the statement said.It added that Bhugwandass could no longer live at home and required round-the-clock care. The statement described his death as the loss of a powerful voice who refused to stay silent in the face of injustice.Just two days before his death, the Stichting Ambulance Wens (Ambulance Wish Foundation), a Dutch non-profit that fulfils final wishes for seriously ill and immobile people, shared photographs of Bhugwandass enjoying a beach photoshoot with his carers and loved ones.“A fierce, but also very beautiful wish. Being this sick at 28 is unimaginable. Right then, photos together with the people you love are incredibly valuable,” the organisation wrote alongside the pictures.From painful experiences in youth care to becoming an activistBhugwandass' campaign for change was shaped by his own experiences growing up. He had spoken about a difficult childhood and the challenges he faced as a teenager, including gender dysphoria, depression and suicidal thoughts. He spent time in youth care institutions, where he later said he experienced isolation and a lack of emotional support.In a 2019 interview with local media, he described feeling as though he was “locked up” in the institutions.“You could be taken to an isolation room for the slightest thing,” he said, recalling how group leaders often felt more like security guards than people he could approach for help.“Not like people I could turn to with my problems. While what I really needed was someone who would stand by my side,” he added.Those experiences led Bhugwandass to campaign for better treatment of children and teenagers in the youth care system. He also carried out peer-led research, interviewing dozens of former residents who had experienced isolation in psychiatric wards.The research found that vulnerable children were kept in extreme isolation for an average of 20 to 21 hours a day. His activism helped bring the issue into the political spotlight, with the Dutch House of Representatives adopting a motion calling for the closure of strict isolation wards in youth care institutions.Named Amsterdammer of the Year in 2022Bhugwandass received wider recognition for his work in 2022 when he was named Amsterdammer of the Year by then-mayor Femke Halsema. He was also known for becoming a prominent face of transgender pride in the Netherlands, including appearing shirtless on billboards in a campaign that drew attention to his visible self-harm scars.Speaking after receiving the award, he said his connection with the city made the recognition particularly meaningful.“Because I am very attached to my city. It means a lot to me to know that it is mutual,” he said.Following his death, Halsema shared an emotional tribute, recalling the impression he had made on her from their first meeting.“Sometimes there are people who change your life. Gradually, not with a bang. From the very first moment I met Jason, I have loved him. Because of his giftedness, his courage, and his incredible perseverance,” she said.She also spoke of her sadness over the injustices he had experienced, saying she felt compassion for “the life stolen from him that prevented him from truly flourishing”.“How Jason deserved that. And how our society deserved that,” she added.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: UK sanctions top Myanmar military leaders after Rohingya genocide ruling
articles.summary: The UK is joined by several other nations in recognising an ICJ ruling that Myanmar carried out genocide.
articles.body:
The UK has sanctioned five senior Myanmar military leaders after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that the country had carried out genocide against the Rohingya minority – marking the first time a state has been found guilty of the crime .

A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma.

The UK is joined by several other countries in acknowledging the ICJ ruling, including Australia, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and Canada.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: "Our response to a crime as profoundly shocking as genocide must reflect our values and must be matched by clear action."

Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications

The senior military leaders facing sanctions are Myo Htut Hlaing, Myo Min Tun, Myat Thet Oo, Kyaw Soe and Kyaw Swar Oo.

Miliband added that Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing , who was sanctioned by the UK in 2021, is "directly responsible for many of the atrocities that have happened" as he was head of the military at the time of the genocide in 2017.

He said: "Myanmar must stop ongoing violations, investigate, prosecute and punish perpetrators, and prevent such an atrocity from ever happening again."

Miliband also called for an "immediate pause in hostilities to enable humanitarian aid to get through, a stop to air strikes on civilians, and the release of political prisoners, as well as dialogue towards an inclusive political settlement".

The foreign secretary confirmed that new legislation would be passed to stop the supply of aviation fuel to the country, which was known as Burma until 1989.

Last week, he expelled Myanmar's defence attaché after the ICJ ruled the country had committed genocide during the brutal military campaign in 2017.

He told MPs on Monday the UK would raise the issue at the UN Security Council this week, and there would be a dedicated meeting in a fortnight.

The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.

The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention .

In its ruling last week, the court determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were murdered during the clearance operation in the western Rakhine state that borders Bangladesh and the Bay of Bengal. Myanmar denied the claims against it.

Reports said that entire villages were burnt down, and that women and girls were raped.

Miliband said more than 1.2 million refugees fled and were being supported by Bangladesh.

Myanmar's leader during the genocide, Aung San Suu Kyi , was deposed by the military in 2021.

MPs heard that air strikes and violence from the Arakan army were still happening.

articles.title: Iran flogs female singer and four members of concert team over her performance without hijab
articles.summary: Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi was lashed 74 times on Monday over a performance in which she appeared without the mandatory hijab, according to defense attorney Mostafa Nili, cited by Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO).
articles.body: Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi was lashed 74 times on Monday over a performance in which she appeared without the mandatory hijab, according to defense attorney Mostafa Nili, cited by Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO). Four members of her concert team also received 74 lashes each, IHRNGO said on X, citing Nili. The sentences were carried out at the Sentence Enforcement Unit of the Qom Prosecutor’s Office against Ahmadi, concert organizer Mohsen Lashkari and musicians Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri and Amir-Ali Pirnia. The case followed the online release of Ahmadi’s “Caravanserai Concert,” filmed in December 2024 at the historic Deir-e Gachin Caravanserai near Qom, a Shiite holy city that is home to numerous Islamic seminaries and is considered a bastion of religious conservatism. (The Persian term caravanserai refers to ancient fortified waystations used by travelers and traders.) A video of the performance, which had no live audience, showed Ahmadi singing alongside male musicians. She wore a long black sleeveless dress with her hair uncovered in defiance of Iran’s mandatory hijab rules. Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of IHRNGO, told CNN that Ahmadi’s clothing was an important factor in the punishment, but he said the prosecution also related to her singing publicly and, more broadly, her challenge to Iranian authorities. Shortly after the video was released, Iran’s judiciary-affiliated Mizan News Agency said authorities had opened a case against Ahmadi and members of the production team over what it described as an “illegal concert.” It said the performance did not comply with the country’s “legal and religious standards.” A court convicted the five of “offending public decency” through the production and dissemination of what it described as vulgar and immoral online content. In addition to flogging, they received two-year bans on artistic and musical activities and foreign travel. An appeals court upheld the ruling in September. Amnesty International has described flogging as a cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment. The human rights group accused Iranian authorities in a report last year of increasingly using arbitrary detention, prosecution and flogging against singers, journalists and women’s rights activists who challenge compulsory veiling. The punishment comes amid continuing pressure on female performers in Iran. Singer Hiva Seyfizadeh was sentenced by a lower court to four years in prison for “encouraging corruption and prostitution” after performing traditional Iranian music in Tehran in February 2025. Seyfizadeh said in a video posted on social media in August that she sang only several verses by renowned 13th-century Persian poet Saadi Shirazi, and she questioned how the performance could constitute encouragement of corruption or prostitution. She said she intends to appeal. Iranian authorities did not immediately comment on the reported implementation of the flogging sentences.

articles.title: US escalates sanctions on Iran, targets ‘shadow banking’ networks
articles.summary: US Treasury sanctions over two dozen Iranian entities, citing efforts to disrupt Tehran’s global financial activities.
articles.body:
The United States has launched another wave of sanctions against Iran under its Operation Economic Outcast, a move that comes shortly after US President Donald Trump threatened renewed military action next year.

The Department of the Treasury announced on Monday that it had targeted more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel with sanctions “in a sweeping effort to disrupt Iran’s global shadow banking networks”.

“Iran’s shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime,” said US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent.

The US Treasury claimed these entities help Iran “move billions of dollars through the international financial system to provide the regime access to foreign currency despite comprehensive sanctions”.

Bessent also vowed the “Treasury will continue dismantling these illicit networks until we have buried the head of the snake.”

The Central Bank of Iran oversees the designated entities, according to the statement .

The designated entities include an Iran-based company named “Rahbar Bazargani Nesim Baharan Qeshm Company (Nesim Baharan)”, which the Treasury claims worked closely with Iranian exchange houses and their front companies to facilitate transactions on behalf of Sarmayeh Bank’s Iranian clients, which include major Iranian petrochemical companies.

In addition , “Mina Fashki and Partners Exchange Company (Fashki Exchange) and Mellat Exchange Company” and a number of their owners and employees were designated.

The US claimed earlier this month that its sanctions campaign had pushed Iran’s rial to new lows and driven inflation to about 90 percent.

AP reported that Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran still hoped diplomacy could end its nine-month war with the US, while President Trump said Iran wanted a deal, but one that was not acceptable to him.

Fox News said Trump told its chief foreign correspondent that he was “inclined to order military strikes against Iran after the new year if the two countries fail to reach an agreement”.

The remarks came as diplomatic efforts continued to end a conflict that has destabilised the Middle East, disrupted shipping, driven up global energy prices, and drawn in countries across the region.

articles.body: For years, the relationship between Prince Harry and the royal family has been under the spotlight, with little indication that the differences between the brothers or the wider family are close to being resolved. But amid the continuing estrangement, a reported gesture from King Charles towards Meghan Markle has offered a possible sign of communication behind closed doors.According to former BBC royal correspondent Jennie Bond, the King reached out to his daughter-in-law after her estranged father, Thomas Markle, was arrested in the US earlier this month. Speaking to Sky News, Bond suggested that Charles expressed sympathy for Meghan as she dealt with the difficult situation.The reported conversation comes at a particularly sensitive time for the Sussexes. While there may be communication between Harry, Meghan and the King, Bond said there was no sign of a similar breakthrough between Harry and his elder brother, Prince William.King Charles checks in on Meghan MarkleBond said she believed Charles had contacted Meghan after Thomas Markle's arrest on November 6, adding that the exchange could be a positive sign for the future.“I'm pretty sure that the King communicated with Meghan after her father was arrested and showed sympathy for her in that predicament. According to Bond, the King has remained loyal to William, who has stood by him, while also keeping his relationship with Harry on reasonable terms.“I've no doubt that [...] it's very, very difficult for Charles to try to keep both sons on board, and he has great loyalty towards William, who has stuck by him all this time. But I think actually that Charles has done a pretty good job of that, and he's on reasonable terms with both his sons,” she said.Thomas Markle's arrest brings fresh distress for MeghanThe reported communication between Charles and Meghan comes after a difficult turn of events involving her father. Thomas Markle, 82, was arrested in Florida on November 6 on a federal charge involving the alleged possession of child sexual abuse material. He denies the allegations.Investigators reportedly seized around 78 items from two storage units in California. Thomas was initially released under electronic monitoring but was later returned to custody after prosecutors alleged that he had cut off his ankle tag. His next preliminary hearing is scheduled for December 1, although the date could change if he is indicted before then.Meghan has previously spoken about the emotional impact of the allegations against her father, saying she was “deeply distressed”. articles.title: Missile on truck in Llangollen goes viral on TikTok
articles.summary: Adrian Hyde and his wife Janette spent years talking about owning a military vehicle.
articles.body:
A 20ft-long Cold War era missile perched on the back of a truck in a field has become a hit on TikTok - and revealed a love story behind it.

Photos and videos of the striking sight near Llangollen, Denbighshire, spread across social media, prompting speculation, theories and curious comments from people wondering how it got there and why.

But for the man who owns it, the story has nothing to do with secret military operations or preparations for war - it is about him using an unusual hobby to honour his late wife.

Adrian Hyde, 59, admits it has now "all just snowballed and I've got carried away" and has spent about £200,000 on numerous vehicles.

Military enthusiasts Adrian and his wife Janette spent years talking about owning a military vehicle and planned to buy a tank as a joint 50th birthday present.

"We had all the area and ground ready, the driveway ready. We knew exactly where we were going to buy it from. We were going to buy a Russian one from Poland," said Adrian.

But this dream was put on hold when Janette was diagnosed with cancer in 2016.

Despite having cancer three times, Adrian said she never lost her determination and the couple "kept saying 'we'll eventually get that tank'. I think that's what kept us going".

Janette died in January 2025 at the age of 57, and Adrian found himself returning to their shared dream and bought the tank three months later.

"The first week after she passed, I said 'I'm going to get that tank she wanted'."

Adrian bought a CVRT scimitar and had it restored by "some military guys in Rugby" who made it road legal.

Then, after getting a call from a military vehicles company telling him they had an armoured Land Rover, he bought that as well.

Adrian said word got round about his collection, leading to a call from a friend saying he had a 1957 AFS Bedford RL missile launcher and a Thunderbird missile for sale.

But because the driveway was full, he asked his friend John if he could put the missile launcher in his field, about 100 yards from his house and he said yes.

Adrian said the bug then got him and he bought a Special Forces Polaris 6 MRZR 4 , which is a project for next summer, with the collecting and restoration helping him cope with his grief.

"I'll be in the front room and look at the tank and think: 'That's part of you dear. That's Janbabes sitting there'."

The unusual sight quickly attracted attention locally before exploding online after a video posted by a hiker and content creator went "absolutely viral" on TikTok and Instagram.

Adrian said: "I've had people ringing me about it. I've got loads of people trying to get friendly on Facebook. It's gone crazy.

"To me it's natural, I have always grown up with military kit, but I suppose it is different."

He said many people have commented saying the missile was live, but that was "ludicrous".

"It's all inactive. It's from the 1950s but in mint condition," he said.

The Thunderbird was withdrawn from service in the 1980s, according to the Imperial War Museum.

"The missile is a Thunderbird missile from the Cold War era, but everything has been stripped off it.

"The inside is hollow. It's got the original outside shell but the inside all the electronics, explosives, jets, they've all been taken off and decommissioned."

A friend made the frame for it and bolted it on the back of a 1957 Bedford truck.

While many may see his military collection as odd, Adrian said it represented a dream he and Janette talked about for years, but never had the chance to realise together.

"It's quite emotional because it was our dream for 10 years. Janette would have loved it."

But the military equipment is not the only way Adrian has honoured his wife.

Following her death, he bought and donated an ambulance to cat charity Candy Tibby Trust in Wrexham, filling it with cat food and raising £3,000 in Janette's memory.

He hopes the sale of the missile and truck can do something similar as his wife was a cat lover.

As for what's next on the list, Adrian said he "doesn't know what yet".

"There are always plans to go buy something. It all depends on what crops up.

Whatever arrives next, its origins can be traced back to a husband keeping alive a dream he once shared with his wife.

articles.title: Florida State makes its move with Glenn Schumann, but nostalgia alone won’t pay for championship roster
articles.summary: Florida State hired Georgia defensive coordinator Glenn Schumann after AD Jeff Purinton gave assurances on spending for the transfer portal and roster.
articles.body: Florida State spent the past few weeks zeroing in on one candidate to replace Mike Norvell. On Monday afternoon, the Seminoles landed their guy, reaching an agreement with Georgia defensive coordinator Glenn Schumann. Both sides agreed to terms, with an expected announcement over the next 24 hours once everything is official. Does the FSU brand still carry the same amount of weight that it did just a decade ago? No, but that doesn’t mean the Seminoles couldn’t attract one of the top names within the coaching circles over the past two seasons. The Seminoles agreed to a five-year deal with the Georgia defensive coordinator, who is expected to stay on with the Bulldogs through the remainder of the 2026 season. ESPN first reported this news. That part will obviously be tested over the next few weeks, as he tries to juggle the two jobs. Hiring a 36-year-old coordinator with no head coaching experience might raise eyebrows among those who haven’t followed Schumann’s career. But when you’ve spent years helping run Georgia’s defense and collecting national championships as an assistant at multiple schools, eventually someone is going to hand you the keys. COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S QUIET SATURDAY TURNS INTO A BIG TEN DISASTER WITH BRUTAL CFP CONSEQUENCES Glenn Schumann was a viable candidate for the North Carolina opening two years ago, before the Tar Heels board of directors decided that the Bill Belichick experience would be the better option. That debacle in Chapel Hill looks worse by the day. For Schumann, it meant staying on Georgia’s sideline and waiting for the next opportunity. Now, the former graduate assistant under Nick Saban gets his shot at leading a program that still has one of the most recognizable names in college football. How highly does Kirby Smart think of Schumann? Bringing him to Athens was a priority when Smart took over at Georgia in 2016. Florida State is now following a path similar to Oregon’s when the Ducks hired Dan Lanning away from Georgia. Similar fire. Similar pedigree. Now comes the challenge of proving he can run the whole operation. It also helped that Florida State athletic director Jeff Purinton knew Schumann from their time together at Alabama under Saban. Can Florida State start winning again under Schumann? If the Seminoles could put together a financial package that would get them back near the top of the spending chart around college football, the coaching would take care of itself under the Georgia defensive coordinator. The problem is that Florida State has struggled over the past few years since going 13-1 and being locked out of the College Football Playoff due to an injury to quarterback Jordan Travis. And, a lot of that comes down to how much money the Seminoles are prepared to spend in hopes of competing for ACC and CFP titles once again. The brand no longer sells itself alone, which is the obvious case around college football over the past five years. Multiple sources told OutKick that this was a main point of emphasis for the Georgia defensive coordinator when deciding on whether to accept the job. After meeting with Florida State officials on Sunday, Schumann needed assurances that the Seminoles were ready to provide him with enough money to attack the transfer portal and load up his roster with enough talent to win immediately. Those assurances were given by athletic director Jeff Purinton, and Glenn Schumann will be tasked with putting together a coaching staff that can also make sure that expensive talent is not wasted. COLORADO BOUGHT INTO 'COACH PRIME'. NOW DEION SANDERS’ LOSING COSTS MORE THAN THE HYPE CAN COVER A team has to be willing to spend money to accrue enough talent through the transfer portal to at least on paper compete for a title. But, there are always risks when it comes to forking up $35 to $45 million for a roster. Look no further than LSU, Texas A&M, Michigan, Ohio State and the countless others who are not in contention for the College Football Playoff this season, but have a roster that's worth over $40 million. COLLEGE FOOTBALL SELLS ANOTHER PIECE OF ITS SOUL WITH CFP OFFICIALLY EXPANDING TO 24 TEAMS But, if the Seminoles are going to get back into the fight under Glenn Schumann, they're going to have to spend. A very important time for Florida State football With the College Football Playoff expanding to 24 teams and the business of college athletics constantly shifting, Florida State needs to start winning again. The discussions about ACC schools potentially leaving for richer conferences over the next five or six years aren’t going away. If the Seminoles want to command more money — whether from another conference or through a future arrangement within the ACC — they need a football program that gives them leverage. Television deals with networks like ESPN and Fox will be heavily discussed within conferences looking to extract additional funds for their future spending. So, if you're going to take part in those conversations, a school had better be in a spot of leverage when it comes to football. That starts on the field. Right now, at this moment, FSU does not have the upper hand. But that doesn’t mean they can't reignite the flame. There is an obvious risk in handing a job this demanding to someone who has never been a head coach. Florida State needs a turnaround, and the pressure to deliver will arrive long before Schumann coaches his first game. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But there aren’t many candidates who can list Saban and Smart as immediate references. The Seminoles have made their bet. Now they need to back it with the money, support and patience required to give it a chance. Florida State wants back into the national conversation. Schumann gets the headset — and the responsibility of making people care again.

articles.title: GTA 6 receives mixed review from Twitch streamer Lacy as he rates the story 6.5 out of 10
articles.summary: GTA 6 may have delivered an impressive gaming experience, but its story has not convinced everyone.
articles.body: GTA 6 may have delivered an impressive gaming experience, but its story has not convinced everyone. Twitch streamer Nick "Lacy" has shared his verdict after completing Rockstar Games' highly anticipated title, praising its massive open world while pointing out problems with its narrative. His review offers an interesting contrast. Although he considers the game a perfect 10, he believes the story takes too long to find its rhythm. Lacy also raised questions about the rewards players receive for completing some of the game's biggest heists.Lacy gives GTA 6 gameplay a perfect score but criticises its slow storyLacy shared his thoughts during a livestream, with a clip from the broadcast circulating on X on November 22, 2026. The CORE member had plenty of praise for the freedom GTA 6 offers players, particularly its exploration, side activities and interactions.He believes the game's open-world experience has enormous potential, especially with GTA Online expected to expand the experience further.Explaining his ratings, Lacy said:"GTA 6, I will give it a 10 out of 10 game. I will give GTA 6 story a 6.5 out of 10. I think the game and the free roam, the side quests, all of the interactions are crazy. I think there is going to be so much, like, things you can do. There are infinite things that you can find. Online is going to be crazy."However, the story was a different experience for the streamer. Lacy felt the opening chapters moved too slowly, making it harder for him to stay engaged. According to him, the narrative improved significantly after roughly 65 to 70 per cent of the game.He also questioned the financial rewards tied to major heists, arguing that the payouts did not match the scale of the missions."The story, for me, was a little slow in the beginning, until about the 65-70% mark, then it got really good. I will say - I was a little disappointed in the beginning because of how slow it was, but then it got really, really good at the end. Obviously, the only critique I would really have to the heist and the story is I wish you got the money from the heist. Like, I'm doing $10 million, $15 million heist, killing thousands of people, and I'm only getting $100,000? So, I don't know."GTA 6 becomes Lacy's first completed story-mode gameInterestingly, Lacy revealed that GTA 6 was the first narrative-driven game he had played from beginning to end without stopping.Despite his complaints, the experience clearly left a positive impression on him."But, overall, I'd say GTA 6 - 10 out of 10 game; 6.5 out of 10 story - for me, personally. But this is the first story-mode game that I ever sat down and continuously played and fully completed. So, definitely going to remember this, and I did enjoy, I'm going to be honest. I did enjoy it. There were some down moments, some boring moments for me, but it was actually a lot of fun."His comments highlight the difference between an engaging open world and a compelling storyline. While Lacy was not entirely satisfied with the narrative, GTA 6 managed to keep him playing until the credits rolled.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Borno school enrolment nearly doubles after years of conflict
articles.summary: Despite rising enrolment, violence, displacement and poverty keep children out of school in northeastern state.
articles.body:
Maiduguri, Nigeria – During years of Boko Haram violence, Maryam Umar’s school in Baga, a town in northeastern Nigeria’s Borno State, was forced to close as violence displaced families and disrupted education across the region.

The closure of the Higher Islamic College in Baga in the Kukawa Local Government Area was part of a wider crisis that deprived thousands of children of regular schooling.

With educational activities now resuming, Umar, a teacher, welcomed efforts to reopen schools and provide learning materials, telling Al Jazeera that the interventions were helping restore education in communities devastated by years of conflict.

Across Borno, authorities said school enrolment has risen sharply as damaged classrooms are repaired and families are encouraged to send their children back to school.

Enrolment in public and private schools reached 1,418,279 learners in 2025, up from 766,551 during the 2017-2018 academic session, according to the state government.

Yet officials estimated that almost 800,000 children remain out of school, highlighting the challenges facing a state where more than a decade of conflict has displaced communities and devastated public services.

The figures suggest progress in expanding access but reveal little about regular attendance, teaching quality or whether children who have missed years of education are catching up.

Borno has been at the centre of Boko Haram violence since the armed group launched its campaign in northeastern Nigeria in 2009.

Schools were among the institutions affected as attacks, displacement and a prolonged lack of security forced families to abandon their homes. In some communities, education became impossible as classrooms closed and teachers and pupils fled.

The state government has made school reconstruction a priority, building new facilities and rehabilitating classrooms damaged by conflict and flooding.

“In response, our administration has constructed 104 new schools and rehabilitated 2,931 classrooms and related facilities,” Governor Babagana Umara Zulum said during the commissioning of educational projects in Maiduguri in March.

According to the governor, the estimated number of out-of-school children has fallen from about 2.2 million at the height of the crisis to fewer than 800,000.

Borno Commissioner for Education, Science, Technology and Innovation Lawan Abba Wakilbe said the increase in enrolment reflects renewed confidence among parents.

But increased enrolment does not necessarily mean children are attending regularly or receiving the support they need after years of disrupted learning.

The available figures also provide little indication of whether the supply of qualified teachers and learning materials has kept pace with the growing number of pupils.

For 12-year-old Fatima Mahmud Umar, a student at the Junior Secondary School One in Maiduguri, education offers an opportunity to pursue ambitions that years of violence have threatened for children across Borno.

Wearing a blue and white chequered hijab and her school uniform, Fatima spoke to Al Jazeera about her hopes for the future.

She expressed gratitude to her parents for supporting her education and said she hopes to become a good ambassador for her community.

Fatima also welcomed government investment in schools, including efforts to support both Islamic and Western education.

But many children across Borno have yet to regain access to regular schooling.

Violence, displacement and poverty continue to create obstacles, particularly for families struggling to rebuild their lives after years of upheaval.

Even where schools have reopened, children who missed months or years of lessons may struggle to catch up with their peers while teachers must accommodate pupils with widely different levels of preparation.

For returning students, enrolment is only the first step. Their prospects also depend on whether schools can provide the support needed to help them progress.

The challenge is particularly pressing in rural communities, where distance, violence and limited resources can make regular schooling difficult.

In the Gubio Local Government Area, residents have raised concerns about children who remain outside formal education despite the government’s reconstruction efforts.

Bukar Abdullahi, 49, highlighted the need to enrol more children during a town hall meeting in Gubio.

While commending the state government for investing in education, Abdullahi drew attention to the difficulties facing rural communities.

For families living far from functioning schools, distance can remain an obstacle. Financial pressures and concerns about safety may also affect decisions about whether children attend.

Although the government’s figures suggest improved access, they do not show how evenly progress is distributed between urban centres and rural communities.

Addressing those disparities will require more than classrooms. Schools also need qualified teachers, learning materials and measures to help families keep their children enrolled.

Alongside conventional schools, Borno authorities are seeking to widen educational opportunities through Arabic and Islamic institutions.

Through the Borno State Arabic and Sangaya Education Board, the government is working to integrate aspects of traditional Islamic learning into a system offering recognised qualifications and pathways to further study.

The establishment of Higher Islamic Colleges is part of that effort.

“This intervention reflects our commitment to building an inclusive education system that integrates spiritual development with academic and vocational advancement,” Zulum said.

According to the governor, the institutions follow a curriculum approved by the National Board for Arabic and Islamic Studies that allows students to pursue recognised qualifications.

The initiative aims to expand opportunities for children whose families favour Islamic education, but its impact will depend on whether institutions can reach underserved communities and provide adequate teaching and resources.

More recent government statistics indicate further expansion of Borno’s education system although differences in the categories counted make direct comparisons difficult.

The state’s annual school census, released in September, recorded 1,801,295 learners across the wider education sector.

Separately, enrolment in public primary and secondary schools stood at about 1.3 million during the 2025-2026 academic session.

Those figures cover different categories from the 1,418,279 learners recorded across public and private schools in 2025 and cannot be directly compared to establish the precise rate of growth.

The government’s estimate that nearly 800,000 children remain out of school also requires context. Without consistent information on the age groups and methodology used, the reported decline from 2.2 million cannot be independently assessed from the figures provided.

Beyond enrolment, questions remain about attendance, teacher availability and learning outcomes, particularly for children whose education was interrupted by conflict.

For teachers such as Umar in Baga, the resumption of educational activities marks a change from the years when violence forced schools to close. For children such as Fatima in Maiduguri, access to education offers opportunities that years of violence have threatened to take away.

But for the hundreds of thousands still outside classrooms, Borno’s educational recovery remains unfinished.

For Wakilbe, the increase in enrolment is nevertheless a sign that families are beginning to regain confidence in the education system.

“When you look at where we started, 766,551 learners in 2017-2018, and see where we are today, this is not just a number. It is evidence that parents and communities once again trust our schools with their children’s future,” he said.

articles.title: Trump calls to ‘expedite’ US federal executions, blasts Gavin Newsom
articles.summary: The US president used his podium to attack the California governor for a decision to commute 548 death sentences.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has reaffirmed his support for the death penalty in an event that doubled as a platform to attack one of his most visible critics, California Governor Gavin Newsom.

On Monday, Trump spoke at the Department of Justice in Washington, DC, where he was joined by the families of crime victims and his attorney general, Todd Blanche.

“The ultimate crimes deserve the ultimate punishment,” Trump said of the death penalty, calling it a cornerstone of “ virtually every society throughout history, at least every successful society”.

“Under the Trump administration, we are bringing it back, and we will not stop in our pursuit of justice. We will not yield.”

He concluded the appearance by signing a presidential directive ordering the Department of Justice to seek the death penalty in murder cases involving children, rape and human trafficking.

The directive also pushes for the attorney general to “expedite” executions for those on federal death row.

As part of his speech, Trump called on Congress to pass the Just Punishment for Murder Act, a bill sponsored by Republican Representative Brandon Gill, which the president said would “strengthen the death penalty in America”.

But he dedicated much of his remarks to slamming Newsom, a Democrat widely seen as a possible contender for the 2028 presidential race.

Newsom’s second term as governor will end on January 4. Under California term limits, he was ineligible to run again in the 2026 midterm elections.

Still, the governor and former San Francisco mayor has carved a national profile for himself as a proxy for Democrats during high-stakes political campaigns — and as a critic of Trump.

Trump, however, zeroed in on one of Newsom’s final major actions while in office: commuting the sentences of those on California’s death row.

On November 5, two days after the midterms, Newsom announced that the 548 people sentenced to death in California would instead be sentenced to life without the possibility of parole.

He described the action as an extension of the moratorium on executions he put in place after taking office in 2019.

“I could not remain true to my values and oversee the killing of people with death warrants in California,” he wrote in an open letter.

He nevertheless denounced the harm the 548 people had caused.

“Many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die,” Newsom wrote. “But as Governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them.”

He called on Californians to let the 548 people “die in obscurity” while remembering their victims.

Trump, however, framed the mass commutation as an effort to help “evil monsters” escape justice.

“This afternoon, we come together to stand against the travesty and to wrap our arms around the families of victims who were so cruelly betrayed by bad government and our political system,” Trump said.

The president proceeded to launch barbs at Newsom, calling him “ a terrible governor” who “ stole away the only closure” the victims’ families “might ever have”.

He then invited several family members on stage to denounce Newsom’s decision.

“ You took the only justice we had and left families feeling abandoned by the state that promised to protect us,” Sandra Friend, the mother of eight-year-old murder victim Michael Lyons, said in her remarks, directed at Newsom.

In anticipation of Monday’s news conference, Newsom also released statements from families that supported his choice.

“When victims are this divided, the death penalty shouldn’t be the answer. Victims deserve so much more than a promise of justice through vengeance,” Jess Nichol, the sister of murder victim Polly Klaas, said in one of the statements.

“They deserve counselling, medical care, financial support, and a justice system that helps them heal. I want something better for survivors: real, tangible support.”

The tit-for-tat between Newsom and Trump comes as support for the death penalty has slumped in recent years.

A November poll released by the research firm Gallup found that 49 percent of US adults support the death penalty, the lowest rate since 1971.

Opponents of the death penalty have frequently pointed to the prevalence of botched executions and the possibility that innocent people may be executed.

The Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit, has found that approximately 202 people formerly on death row were later found to be wrongfully convicted. The exoneration rate, it said, was one for every eight people executed in the US.

Death penalty cases also typically tend to result in longer court battles and higher costs.

Before Newsom’s mass commutation, California reportedly had the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere, representing roughly a quarter of the country’s death sentences.

Newsom’s successor, Governor-elect Xavier Becerra, has pledged to continue the death penalty moratorium once sworn in.

But that policy puts California at odds with a push under Trump to embrace the death penalty and expand execution methods.

Upon taking office for a second term on January 20, 2025, Trump signed the first of several executive orders aimed at “restoring the death penalty”.

He pushed to have execution be the de facto punishment for the murder of law enforcement officers, as well as for murder cases where undocumented immigrants are the defendants.

In April, the Trump administration also said it would prioritise the use of the death penalty by expanding the acceptable methods for federal execution, including firing squads .

In October, Trump’s Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that one execution by firing squad — that of the Fort Hood shooter, Nidal Hasan — would be livestreamed to the public, prompting backlash.

Trump later walked back the announcement, amid reports that he did not realise Hassan was in a wheelchair.

During his first term, Trump oversaw 13 federal executions, the most of any president in decades. In Monday’s speech, he framed such punishments as “common sense”.

“ When it comes to defending the lives and safety of American people, there can be no compromise,” he said.

articles.title: BBC exposes Whitby dog breeder selling sick puppies for £2k each
articles.summary: The breeder's rating was downgraded but he continued to advertise as five-star, investigation finds.
articles.body:
When Katie Thornton paid £2,000 for a nine-week-old puppy for her son, she knew it was a premium price - but was happy to be doing business with a "legit", council-approved breeder.

But Ozzy the Dobermann pup started coughing in the car on the way home, and within 48 hours he was in a veterinary hospital receiving urgent treatment for pneumonia.

Since then, his ongoing health problems mean Katie has racked up more than £5,000 in vet bills.

A BBC investigation has found the breeder had been stripped of his five-star rating two months before selling several sick puppies, but continued to advertise as five-star.

We have also found at least 15 other breeders in England advertising puppies alongside claims their star rating is higher than it really is.

An expert reviewing our findings - including undercover footage we recorded at the breeder's home - said the investigation exposes a nationwide "wild west" of dog licensing, making it "easy for consumers to be scammed".

The breeder has not responded to our request for comment.

When Katie visited the premises of Mikjulora Dobermanns in Whitby, North Yorkshire, she said the puppies' mother "didn't look very well" and was "skinny" and "shaking".

But she felt the breeder, Michael Estill, was "pushing me to buy Ozzy" so she paid for him and took him home on the spot.

Katie defended her decision because she had done extensive research to check the business was "legit".

The mother-of-one, from Harrogate, said she had checked his licence number and read through his website and online adverts, which said he had decades of experience and a "five-star" breeding licence.

In England, local councils grant breeders in their area a licence and star rating dependent on welfare standards.

Vet reports for North Yorkshire Council from August and December 2025, seen by the BBC, cited dozens of concerns with Estill's business, including:

"Poor" living conditions "akin to a prison", with dogs kept in cages, stacked on top of each other, that were too small for them to turn around in

Deteriorating health and welfare of "sad" dogs

Puppies for sale not matching descriptions - "in other words it is a scam"

Prospective buyers "very vulnerable to unsuspectingly purchasing unhealthy puppies"

The business was "more or less a puppy farm masquerading as an honest and conscientious breeder. This must stop"

Estill "bullied" a local vet to perform an "unnecessary" Caesarean section on one of his dogs, to reduce the time he would have to spend monitoring her

His "demanding" behaviour led the practice to give him several doses of a powerful stimulant which he gave to one of his dogs at home - which the vet considered to be "negligent"

He had a three-year-old dog euthanised because he suspected her to have a neurological condition, despite the vet encouraging him to get diagnostic tests and specialist treatment first.

Following the reports, which concluded that the business was "functioning outside the law", the council renewed Estill's licence in January but downgraded his rating from five-star (the highest standards) to one-star (minor failings).

Dr Caroline Allen, founder of Pet Lighthouse and former RSPCA chief veterinary officer, said she was "surprised and shocked" that the business kept its licence.

A North Yorkshire Council spokesperson said the threshold for revoking a licence "was not considered to have been met on the evidence available".

They added: "We take animal welfare very seriously and investigate concerns brought to our attention.

"Following the veterinary inspection reports, we have continued to work with the licence holder to address the identified concerns and are satisfied that standards have significantly improved, resulting in a higher level of animal welfare at the premises."

The BBC has evidence that Estill continued to sell puppies while claiming on his website and in person that he was five-star rated.

While Estill has since updated his website homepage, he has not updated the metadata, which means when his business is searched for online the five-star claim still appears alongside a link to his site.

There is no official list of licensed breeders and their star ratings, and not all councils publish them, so Katie took his word for it.

"If I would've known he was a one-star breeder, I would've never even gone to the property. I wouldn't have bought a dog off a one-star breeder," she said, adding that she wanted to see Estill's licence revoked.

Kat Durrant's dog Bentley died aged three in 2022 of a heart condition known as dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM).

Within days of bringing him home from Mikjulora Dobermanns, Kat says Bentley was "really poorly".

"The vet asked me if I had got the dog from a puppy farm because of his condition," she added.

Three years later, Kat had Bentley put to sleep as his weak heart was "giving up" and he was struggling to breathe.

"Bentley suffered his whole life because of everything he'd been through when he was young," she said.

Kat, from Manchester, set up a Facebook group where other people who had bought dogs from Estill could share their experiences.

Including Kat, owners of 17 dogs mentioned in the group said the pets had died before the age of eight, including 10 below the age of four.

Several others claimed their dogs were sick at a young age but survived.

The vet report from December 2025 said Estill was not correctly testing his dogs for DCM despite his website saying that he did test.

The report said the fact that Estill did "nothing" when customers told him about DCM diagnoses was "truly the hallmark of a breeder who does not care about the welfare or improving the breed".

Michelle Paton, who lives in Edinburgh, bought her puppy Cruz a week before Katie bought Ozzy.

He had a cough "as soon as he came through the front door" and was diagnosed with pneumonia and possible heart failure a few weeks later.

Michelle was frustrated to discover Kat's Facebook group and felt Estill's licence should have been revoked "years ago".

"If somebody was actually doing their job properly then they would have put an end to him breeding a long time ago," she said.

Caroline Housam, from York, bought her puppy Roxy the day before Katie bought Ozzy.

Roxy started coughing in the car on the journey home.

When Caroline took Roxy to the vet she said she was told there were problems with her glands, and later they found she had a limp and ulcers in her eyes.

She is having ongoing treatment and tests.

"I'm actually angry because I look at my dog and I'm thinking, 'I don't know what lies ahead'," said Caroline.

"When you listen to what other people have said [on Facebook] who have had [dogs] bred from him, her chances of living until two are slim."

To corroborate the claims made, the BBC sent undercover reporters to film at Estill's home, posing as potential puppy buyers.

Estill refused to show us where the puppies and their mother slept.

He said he had "another 15 Dobermanns" in cages in a back room and worried that the neighbours would complain if we went in and they started barking.

He offered to show us the space another day and said he had "nothing to hide".

Reviewing our footage, Allen said this refusal was the "most serious concern" and breached regulations.

She added that the eyes of two of the puppies for sale were " not all normal", citing "a number of abnormalities" such as discoloration and the shape of the eye socket.

Looking at a photo of a male pup taken by the BBC, she said: "That is not a healthy dog."

Estill's licence certificate and star rating were also not visibly on display anywhere, despite government rules saying both should be "clearly and prominently displayed" for customers.

BBC research has found at least 15 other breeders in England who are also advertising puppies alongside claims their star rating is higher than the one they have been given by their local authority.

We checked through a list of 806 breeders with a rating between one and four stars.

Of the 573 breeders rated three-star or below (meaning lower standards), we could not find mention of a rating on their websites, social media pages or in online adverts for puppies in 541 cases.

Of the 32 who did mention a rating, 11 had active adverts claiming to be more highly rated than they really were.

Of the 45 four-star rated breeders to mention a rating, four claimed they were five-star in active adverts.

The man accused of tricking his friends out of £50,000

Ex-workers tell of 'chaotic atmosphere' at new £400m prison

One council confirmed a breeder we enquired about did not have a licence at all, another said they could not find the information we needed, and others took weeks to respond.

The list of breeders was provided by Paws on the Doors, an organisation aiming to collate breeders' star ratings across the country in one place. For each of the breeders whose online claims did not match the Paws on the Doors list, we checked with individual councils to verify the up-to-date rating.

Commenting on the BBC's findings, Paws on the Doors co-founder Leigh Grant said the main reason "the scammers exist" was that central government and local councils had "failed" to properly implement the principles of legislation for breeder licensing from 2018.

He said a lack of support for animal welfare had led to a position where breeders can "falsely claim higher standards, without fear of detection".

Allen said our findings showed puppy breeding was "an absolute wild west" and there should be "countrywide teams of inspectors and vets who are properly trained to understand the legislation".

She said: "It is easy for consumers to be scammed, but unfortunately at the heart of this there are really vulnerable animals and puppies."

Amy Thompson-Copsey, senior public affairs officer at Dogs Trust, said potential puppy owners should "trust your instinct" to avoid falling for "financial scams".

"If something seems off, if you feel red flags, just walk away. You don't know what you could be getting into."

A Defra spokesperson said they were committed to ending "low welfare dog breeding" and were consulting on reforms to protect dogs' health and better inform the public on "which breeders they can trust".

The BBC put all allegations to Michael Estill and his wife Julie Estill, who is the named director of Mikjulora on Companies House, but they did not respond.

articles.title: Britain's landlords are getting bigger. A two-tier rental market may follow
articles.summary: Increasing numbers of corporate landlords could usher in big changes for renters
articles.body:
On Christmas Eve 2021, there was a knock on the door of Lexi Levens' rented flat. It was a letter sent by special delivery from the NHS nurse's landlord saying she, her husband, and four children had two months to move out.

"The kids all thought it was a present arriving," she recalls.

Lexi's landlord had used something known then as a Section 21 notice to evict her family without needing to give a reason.

Lexi, along with the housing charity Shelter, went on to lobby the government to improve rights for renters. The Renters' Rights Act, which came into force in May this year, banned Section 21 evictions and also made it illegal to refuse to rent to people based on their status as a family with children.

The landlords Lexi had been renting from at that time were typical of the English housing market — individuals who owned one or a handful of properties.

Many of these small landlords say the Renters' Rights Act has left them feeling squeezed. They also say rising interest rates, new regulations and tax changes (including some in the most recent Budget) are making things harder. Some say they are selling up.

Meanwhile, according to Savills estate agents, 2026 is likely to be another record year for investment from large institutions in what is known in the property industry as build to rent (BTR). This is when big developers build blocks of flats or family housing to rent out, something that is commonplace in parts of Europe and the US. It means that rather than dealing with an individual landlord or letting agent, tenants are instead renting from larger, typically corporate, entities.

So does the shift, as some believe, represent a welcome professionalisation of the UK rental sector? Or will renters increasingly miss the positive elements of the personal touch that small landlords can provide?

According to the latest government survey of private landlords in England, 83% of English landlords own four properties or fewer, representing 51% of tenancies.

And according to 2024 research by real estate agency Savills, around 40% rental homes in the US and Germany are owned by large institutions — be they private firms, listed companies, pension funds, or co-operatives. For the UK, Savills calculated that figure was just 3%.

But the rental market is changing. The trend is most visible in England, where BTR has boomed in large cities and where regulations like the Renters' Rights Act apply, but there are BTR developments in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland too and the devolved nations are also seeing increased regulation on landlords, such as with Scotland's rent controls.

Lexi is pleased with the idea of a sector with stricter rules for landlords and more professional institutions getting involved.

"Anything that takes away from landlords having personal preferences [around choosing who they are or not prepared to rent to]… is a good thing," she says, adding that she believes large, corporate landlords would be less likely to act that way.

Not everyone is convinced BTR landlords are better, though.

Clint Stevenson, a 44-year-old magician for weddings and events, has been renting his one-bedroom flat in Ramsgate for £550 a month for two years. He says he has "the most amazing landlady" — an older woman who he regularly chats to. He sometimes walks her dog and does her shopping as well.

He says he had considered renting from a BTR development, but found the accommodation to be "very industrial and very unpersonal". He also found what was on offer to be expensive compared to what he is used to paying.

"They just look like big, money-grabbing deals," he says.

In Cardiff, Grainger, the UK's largest listed BTR developer, is currently offering a fully-furnished studio flat on the 20th floor of The Copper Works in the city centre with views over the bay for £1,265 a month.

It's a lot more than what is currently on offer on Rightmove, a 15 minute walk away from the city centre – a fully-furnished, ground-floor, one-bedroom flat with a garden for £800 a month.

But tenants in The Copper Works have free access to a gym, a cinema room, a roof terrace, and a games room. There's also free WiFi, a concierge service with a helpline, and other amenities. In addition, the studio flat has an EPC B rating as opposed to an EPC C rating for the one-bedroom flat down the road.

"You have to look at what you're getting for your rent," says Helen Gordon, Grainger's chief executive. She says BTR landlords can offer these services because of their scale. As she puts it: "If you run 11,000 homes, you can afford to invest in systems, processes, people, helplines – that sort of thing – that smaller landlords can't."

Gordon strongly pushes back against suggestions that there is a lack of human connection within BTR, noting that tenants are able to speak with staff whenever they need and that the firm regularly organises events for socialising with other tenants to create a sense of community.

It's a pattern across the BTR sector: a higher price point in exchange for what is marketed as high-quality accommodation and a suite of services — some in the sector even refer to 'customers' rather than 'tenants'.

The number of BTR homes has tripled between 2019 and 2025, and while it represents just 3% of the overall rental market at the moment, Gordon believes it could reach "at least 10%" over the next ten years. "And I think it could go higher," she adds.

"If you've got major institutions that include pension funds, financial institutions, and FTSE 250 companies running the stock, it's easier to hold people to account than lots of disparate people, so you can see why it's attractive [to government]."

A 2012 government-commissioned report concluded that more BTR properties could help increase housing supply and drive economic growth as well as providing tenants with more choice and better quality housing. It recommended central government and councils support the development of BTR through favourable planning decisions and releasing public land.

There is a lot of evidence governments and local authorities listened. Local leaders in big cities – London and Manchester, in particular – have partnered with developers to deliver large housing projects involving, in many cases, the release of public land. Kings Cross in London is a prime example of this and current London Mayor Sadiq Khan's push for BTR development near Transport for London (TFL) land, mostly Tube stations, is another example. As part of that, TfL formed a joint venture with Grainger.

Lucian Cook, head of residential research at Savills, says it's not a matter of looking at one policy, government, or council in particular but more the "policy environment" which has been around since the 2010s.

He points to a series of tax changes, including mortgage interest tax relief changes and higher stamp duty rates for second homes and buy-to-let properties introduced by the Conservatives around 10 years ago, which made the sector less favourable for smaller landlords.

The Renters' Rights Act and more stringent energy efficiency requirements were later introduced. And the last two Budgets have raised taxes on rental income from next year. The tax change applies to individuals who are landlords, not to BTR companies which pay corporation tax, further encouraging professionalisation of the sector.

Yet, while many welcome these changes, others say they are pushing smaller landlords out of the sector. As Cook puts it, there has been more "stick" for small landlords than "carrot" for the BTR sector.

Between 2000 and 2016, a net 2.74 million homes were added to the English rental market in total, according to an analysis of government data by the Joseph Rowntree Foundation. In the 10 years since, a net of just 200,000 have. For renters, it is now less likely that your property is owned by a smaller landlord.

Kevin Barber started off with one rental home. He has since grown this portfolio to 40 properties with his business partner but resents what he sees as the clout of the BTR sector. "The big property companies have got so much financial power and influence with the government," he says.

Many experts, landlord groups, and tenant groups agree that building more housing — whether that's rental housing or housing for sale — would help solve many of the issues in the rental sector.

The thinking goes that building more homes for rent, provided people can afford them, would help deal with the supply crunch that can drive up rental costs and force tenants into lower quality properties. And building more homes for sale, provided people can afford them, would remove those from the market who don't want to rent but are forced into it.

But whether we will actually see more homes being built is another matter. Savills' Cook says BTR development could slow in future as high interest rates and increased building costs continue to hit developers' bottom line. These same factors are why housebuilders say they are building less.

Cook says the current rate of BTR development won't be enough to meet the demand for rental properties on its own, at least not imminently. In addition, while some BTR developers do build cheaper family homes for rent in the suburbs, the sector is largely still building blocks of flats for wealthier renters living in cities.

This raises the possibility that the UK could end up with a two-tier rental market – what Cook describes as the "haves and the have nots" – where high-earning city-dwelling renters have their pick of rental properties but poorer renters in suburbs struggle to find somewhere to live.

Unless the government steps in, possibly by delivering more housing itself or partnering with developers to do so, it might find any positives gained by the Renters' Rights Act are undone by an increasingly fragmented rental market.
