articles.title: No 10 North will face greater scrutiny as Andy Burnham's 10-year plan looms
articles.summary: The work of Number 10 North in Manchester has been kept largely away from the headlines since it opened in July.
articles.body:
The work of Andy Burnham's new Number 10 North office in Manchester has been kept largely away from the headlines since it opened in July.

But the officials based there are mainly focused on two soon-to-be-published documents that could go on to define his time as prime minister.

The first is Burnham's 10-year plan, which is due next month, and which the prime minister says will lay out a path "to where I believe we all want Britain to be".

The second is the 'rewiring the state' white paper, a detailed policy document that will follow in the new year and should give the clearest indication yet of what power Burnham hopes to move away from Westminster to other parts of the country.

But despite Burnham insisting his new Manchester team will be the "engine room" of change, others in government question how much difference they can really make.

There's talk among Labour MPs that the 10-year plan, which has also had significant input from Westminster departments, will not go as far as the prime minister had hoped.

But one official who has seen elements of the plan said it will be "pretty weighty" and include "quite a lot of radicalism".

Number 10 North has been focused on how the plan can deliver on Burnham's pledge to achieve "growth in every postcode".

One major theme is expected to be reindustrialisation, with advisers exploring how to attract businesses to less prosperous towns and cities.

Staff in Manchester are also said to be looking at what parts of the country may not see growth through reindustrialisation – such as some rural and coastal areas – and what the alternative offer for those places could be.

Eyebrows were raised in Whitehall this summer when a government statement said that "local economic growth policy" would be transferred "from HM Treasury directly into No 10 North".

Some saw that as an attempt to disempower the Treasury, but sources there insist that no serious decisions on growth can be made without the department's involvement and approval.

Burnham's Number 10 North goes on multi-million pound hiring spree

'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

When Burnham first announced plans for the Manchester base, he singled out housing as an issue on which it would take the lead.

In a speech last month Number 10 North's deputy director highlighted health, transport and education as other areas it was focused on.

While it's understood the 10-year plan is likely to include long-term ambitions for social care, skills training and council housebuilding, there are doubts within government departments about exactly how involved Number 10 North will eventually be in those areas.

One Whitehall official said "most things" that have been announced as Number 10 North priorities have in practice "stayed with other departments".

They said Number 10 North is "not doing delivery" because it "doesn't have its own resource" and is "underpowered compared to departments" in London.

That is almost half of the around 280 staff members that work for "Number 10 South", a term some advisers are now using for Downing Street.

But even those staffing levels are only a fraction of the numbers employed by other departments.

The Treasury's north of England campus in Darlington, which was set up in 2021, has around 3,000 staff.

John Healey is said to have been particularly impressed with the Darlington campus's record of hiring people who would otherwise not have joined the civil service, something Downing Street hopes to achieve in Manchester too.

Darlington's most senior civil servant, Beth Russell, has been working with Number 10 North to share her experience of how best to set up a new government office outside London.

Prime ministers have for decades been frustrated by how little power Number 10 can sometimes wield within Whitehall, arguing that levers can be pulled but nothing then happens.

One question at the heart of the Number 10 North project is whether it will eventually wield genuine power itself or merely decide which powers to take from Westminster and give to mayors and other regional politicians around the country.

A government source said Number 10 North's current role is "more in convening" people from elsewhere and argued the prime minister would need to choose what he wanted it to do in the future.

They added: "I could see it going two different ways.

"Will it be more delivery or will it be more in the conventional role of Number 10?

"Maybe it's not best placed to do things, but maybe directing and convening are also important things to do."

Regional mayors have been regular visitors of Number 10 North and are set to be earmarked for much more expansive powers in the 'rewiring the state' white paper.

England currently has 14 metro mayors, a number which is likely to be expanded in the coming years.

Sources in both Number 10 and the Treasury say "fiscal devolution" will be a major part of the Burnham agenda.

People close to the prime minister say that is likely to ultimately mean more cash-raising, spending and borrowing power for mayors.

Two of Burnham's early announcements this summer saw mayors given a share of income tax and the ability to introduce a tourist tax for people visiting their areas.

The Treasury believes one of the most underreported elements of Healey's Budget last month was a £1.5bn borrowing facility that will be given to mayors from 2028.

Sources say that in the future projects such as Doncaster-Sheffield Airport, which Healey gave his backing to, could be given the financial go-ahead directly by mayors, without the need for a separate thumbs up from the chancellor.

For now mayors have each been asked to submit a list of projects to Number 10 North, which they feel are being held up by government processes.

Government departments in Westminster have also been asked to identify what areas they are currently responsible for which could potentially be devolved to mayors and other local government officials.

What's less clear is how the prime minister's devolution plans will affect Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland and whether he is keen for them too to adopt a mayoral model.

At a recent meeting in Glasgow, Burnham said he would discuss that further with the leaders of the devolved nations.

He recently rejected a proposal from the First Minister of Wales to devolve more responsibilities over policing and justice.

Away from the gaze of backbench MPs, opposition parties and Westminster journalists, Number 10 North has so far been able to go about its business without drawing much attention.

But as Burnham's long-term plans for the country start to become more clear, the scrutiny faced by his Manchester power base is likely to grow too.

articles.title: Bukele shares details on deaths of Salvadoran troops in Haiti intervention
articles.summary: Bukele’s military intervention in Haiti comes after four Salvadoran technicians were kidnapped by gangs in October.
articles.body:
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele has identified the three soldiers from his Central American country who were killed while on an anti-gang mission in Haiti.

Late on Sunday, Bukele posted on social media that their names were Lieutenant Cristian Daniel Palacios Santos and Corporals Emerson Alexander Zepeda Zelada and Wilber Manuel Serrano Medina.

“Tragically, an accidental explosion during that mission claimed their lives,” Bukele said.

He also described instances in which the men had shown “bravery” in the past.

During “tests in El Salvador”, Bukele said that Zepeda Zelada and Serrano Medina took quick action to disarm a grenade lodged in a drone.

“It was not possible to steer the drone toward a completely safe area for it to crash,” Bukele said. “They were fully aware of the immense risk they were taking, yet they chose to act to protect others. And they succeeded.”

According to Bukele, Palacios Santos was admired for recently taking control during a “critical moment” in an operation in which some contractors allegedly retreated.

“He acted with speed and determination, managing to save several lives, including those of his own colleagues,” Bukele wrote. “We all applaud his bravery.”

Bukele also used his post to pledge that Salvadoran troops who want to leave Haiti could do so immediately without facing reprisals.

The Salvadoran soldiers killed last week were among 2,500 deployed to Haiti last month after four of their own went missing during an October 18 attack in gang-held territory. They have not yet been found.

Bukele said that his government would award the families of the three soldiers killed on Friday $200,000 in addition to a monthly income.

He also stressed that any soldier who wants to leave Haiti immediately may do so “without fear of reprisal and without concern that their return might jeopardise the mission, as many of their comrades have volunteered to relieve anyone who wishes to be relieved”.

Salvadoran troops have come under increased scrutiny as experts and the United Nations note they are operating in a largely unilateral way. Thousands of Haitians recently demonstrated to support Bukele.

The agreement between Haiti and El Salvador hasn’t been made public.

“There is no information on the scope and limits of its mission, nor on its accountability mechanisms,” according to a report published Monday by NAL Human Rights, a Netherlands-based consulting company focused on Central American issues.

It noted that, regardless of what that deal stipulates, Salvadoran and international laws require that El Salvador’s armed forces comply with human rights and humanitarian laws.

The report also underscored that the Central American country and the International Criminal Court have jurisdiction to prosecute Salvadoran military personnel if they are accused of war crimes, genocide or crimes against humanity.

More than 20,000 people have been killed in gang-related violence across Haiti in the past five years.

US lawmakers demand answers about the situation in Haiti

The deaths of the Salvadoran soldiers come as local and international forces fight powerful gangs entrenched in Martissant, a community located in a key corridor that links Haiti’s capital to the country’s western and southern regions.

Dozens of suspected gang members have been killed since last week as the battle in Martissant continues, police have said.

It is the first major operation in Martissant in the more than five years that gangs have controlled it.

As Haitian police and others continue to battle gangs in Martissant, a UN-backed gang suppression force said it killed several suspected gang members on Sunday as part of ongoing operations in Tabarre and Cite Soleil, located in Port-au-Prince, and in the northern town of Gros Morne.

As fighting intensifies, two Democratic lawmakers on Monday accused the administration of US President Donald Trump of failing to “name and sanction the political and economic elite fueling Haiti’s insecurity”.

The concern was outlined in a letter penned by New Hampshire Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and New York Representative Gregory Meeks, the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

“At a time when the Haitian people are preparing to vote for the first time in over a decade, Congress, the American public and the Haitian people deserve transparency about the nature and scale of collusion between gangs and their political and economic support networks,” they said.

The letter was addressed to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

Haiti is scheduled to hold the first round of elections in July 2027. Among the candidates running are some previously sanctioned by the United States and Canada.

articles.title: Israeli minister approves return of Flydubai flights to Tel Aviv
articles.summary: Final resumption of carrier’s route between Dubai and Tel Aviv depends on Israeli security authorities’ approval.
articles.body:
Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev has approved the resumption of Flydubai flights to Tel Aviv, according to Israeli media, almost two months after an onboard incident where a co-pilot was accused of attacking his captain.

Regev made the announcement on Monday, though Israel’s security authorities’ approval is still required for flights to resume. The ministry expects operations to resume within a week or two, Israeli media said.

The minister’s approval comes after talks between Israeli officials, led by ministry Director-General Moshe Ben-Zaken, and Emirati aviation officials took place in Dubai on November 16.

Authorities discussed potential security measures that would allow for airlines to fully resume flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv.

“The delegation today presented Regev with the steps the company has taken in the wake of the incident,” Israeli media reported, citing a transportation ministry statement. “As a result, Regev approved the return of Flydubai, subject to clearance from security authorities.”

“The move is a significant step toward restoring air connectivity between Israel and the UAE and expanding flight options for passengers,” the statement added.

Flydubai halted flights to Tel Aviv on September 30 as it began an investigation into the events that transpired on board a Boeing 737 Max 8. Israeli carriers also stopped running routes to Dubai, making Etihad, which flies to Abu Dhabi, the only carrier flying between the UAE and Israel, according to Israeli media.

The co-pilot, who was identified as an Omani national, was arrested when the plane diverted and made an emergency landing in Tabuk, northwestern Saudi Arabia.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused the co-pilot of trying to crash the plane and of attacking the captain, Smit Machchhar, an Indian national.

The emergency came a day after Netanyahu warned of possible attacks in the lead-up to Israel’s October 27 parliamentary elections.

articles.title: Appeals court renews Trump bid for federal jurisdiction in hush-money case
articles.summary: The ruling could clear the way for Trump to argue prosecutors relied on evidence protected by presidential immunity.
articles.body:
A federal appeals court has revived United States President Donald Trump’s bid to transfer his New York criminal hush-money case to federal court, months after a district judge rejected the effort for a third time.

On Monday, a three-judge panel of the 2nd Circuit Court of Appeals reversed a lower court ruling that had kept the case in New York state court.

In a two-page order, the 2nd Circuit panel said it disagreed with the late US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein’s denial of Trump’s request for the “removal” of his case to federal court.

The appeals court said Hellerstein had “erred in holding that removal is categorically unavailable in a state criminal case” after conviction.

It directed a federal judge in Manhattan to consider whether the proceedings could be brought under federal jurisdiction.

In a written statement provided to The Associated Press news agency, a spokesperson for Trump’s legal team said the president “appreciates the 2nd Circuit’s prompt and correct ruling, as he continues to win against Democrat weaponization of our Justice System”.

Trump has sought to use presidential immunity in federal court to have his conviction overturned. He was convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records in 2024, though he has denied any wrongdoing.

The case stems from a $130,000 “hush money” payment made shortly before the 2016 presidential election to adult film performer Stormy Daniels .

Daniels had claimed she had an affair with the Republican leader while he was married — an allegation he denies — and prosecutors alleged that the money was intended to buy her silence during a tense campaign season.

Trump ultimately won the 2016 presidential election, ushering him into his first term in public office.

The payment was made through Trump’s former lawyer and fixer Michael Cohen. Prosecutors argued that Trump fudged his business records to pass off his reimbursements to Cohen as legal expenses, thereby concealing them from voters.

While falsifying business records is normally a misdemeanour offence, it can be charged as a felony if done in service of another crime. In Trump’s case, prosecutors said he violated state election laws.

In May 2024, a New York jury found him guilty, making Trump the first US president to be convicted of a crime.

At a sentencing hearing in January 2025 — shortly before his second term as president began — Trump received an unconditional discharge, meaning he faced neither imprisonment nor a financial penalty. But his conviction remains on the record.

Why does Trump want the case heard in federal court?

For years, Trump has sought to overturn that conviction.

Monday’s ruling leaves the jury’s guilty verdict intact, but it also clears the way for the president to seek a hearing in federal court.

He is expected to argue that state prosecutors secured his conviction by relying on evidence that would have been shielded by presidential immunity in federal court.

His legal team is likely to point to a landmark 2024 ruling as justification for that argument.

At the time, the Supreme Court’s conservative majority ruled that presidents could enjoy “presumptive immunity” for any “official acts” conducted while in office.

What constitutes an “official act”, however, is an open question. Previously, the Supreme Court had only conferred immunity to actions taken within a president’s constitutional authority.

Monday’s ruling reverses a series of setbacks for Trump’s legal team.

In August, federal judge Hellerstein rejected Trump’s third attempt to transfer the case, finding that the president’s arguments were insufficient to justify moving it out of state court.

Hellerstein, a senior federal judge in Manhattan’s Southern District of New York, died last month at the age of 92.

The move also stalls Trump’s state-level appeal in New York’s Appellate Division, which heard arguments earlier this month but has yet to rule on his challenge.

A federal judge has been directed to rule promptly on whether the case should indeed be transferred from New York state court to federal jurisdiction, although no deadline has been set.

articles.title: Once again, the College Football Playoff selection committee has an opportunity to fix their mistakes
articles.summary: The College Football Playoff committee faces scrutiny as Alabama's best wins once again lost this weekend while Indiana dropped five spots for the same reason.
articles.body: Well, we're back for another week. Tuesday evening, the College Football Playoff selection committee will release their latest top-25 poll, despite our best efforts, and ESPN will host Committee Chair Hunter Yurachek for a post-release interview. And already, they've trotted out Heather Dinich to justify whatever absurdities they have coming for us. But before going into what we can expect, it's worth quickly revisiting how we got here. WILL THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF SELECTION COMMITTEE EMBARRASS ITSELF AGAIN WITH NEW RANKINGS? In week one, the committee's poll consistently overrated SEC teams, with virtually all of them sitting several spots, at least, ahead of where more unbiased, objective metrics-based system placed them. That unsurprising trend continued in week two, and despite the outrage and complaints from fans and analysts about week one's poll, the committee doubled and tripled down. The Indiana Hoosiers dropped five spots, despite sitting out with a bye, and Yurachek's explanation for it was disastrous at best, and disqualifying and insulting at worst. "Every team that Indiana had played to date in the Big Ten all lost and that affected their strength of schedule rank and the committee's review of Indiana," he said. "The quarterback play in general and the offensive play in general is kind of a discussion point of Indiana ... They've won games because of their defense and not their offense." Ignoring everything else, the important note was that Indiana's Big Ten opponents all lost in the same week, hurting their strength of schedule. Then, between week two and week three, the exact same thing happened to the Alabama Crimson Tide. South Carolina lost to an awful Arkansas team by 28 points. Texas A&M lost at home, again. Mississippi State lost its fifth game in a row with yet another defensive disaster class. Kentucky lost its second in a row, as its offense continued to struggle, then LSU lost at home again too. Yurachek and the committee didn't drop the Tide a single spot. Then when asked about it, gave a thoroughly discrediting answer. "Alabama faced a similar circumstance where five of their SEC opponents all lost, but it didn't have the same impact on their strength of schedule that it had on Indiana's strength of schedule," he said. "Actually, it is very minimal for Alabama because of the quality and the strength of schedule of those five teams that lost." There are only a few certainties in life, death, taxes, and the selection committee worshipping at the feet of the Crimson Tide. The good news for fans who want to see some objectivity? The committee has another opportunity this week, thanks to another rough Saturday for the Tide's strength of schedule, to show that they're willing to be unbiased and not play favorites. Again, the stated justification for Indiana dropping five spots was that all the Big Ten teams they played lost in the same week. When that exact scenario played out for Alabama, they did not drop at all. This weekend? It got worse. The Tide's "signature" win thus far was the Kentucky Wildcats. In conference, they also beat LSU, Texas A&M, Vanderbilt, Mississippi State without Kamario Taylor, and South Carolina. Out of conference, they beat Florida State, East Carolina, and Chattanooga. Here's how their primary wins did this past weekend: HERE'S HOW BAD THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF'S SELECTION COMMITTEE RANKINGS ACTUALLY ARE Every single team that provided a "big" win for Alabama and played a competitive program lost. Kentucky's fallen off a cliff, losing three straight games and scoring just 34 combined points. South Carolina showed why their ranking was always based on unjustified assumptions of SEC strength. Vanderbilt and Texas A&M continued to be two of the worst Power 4 teams in the country, LSU was LSU, and Tennessee Tech provided the free SEC November bye week, allowing the Bulldogs to end their five-game losing streak. With these results, here are the records of Alabama's signature wins this year: The combined records of those teams, including FCS wins, is just 37-40. Meanwhile, Alabama lost to the only two elite teams they played, Georgia and Tennessee. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Is that enough? Is that finally enough for the committee to admit they might have made a mistake by assuming that every SEC team deserved to be ranked because they're in the SEC? And that in doing so, they provide undeserved strength of schedule boosts to teams like Alabama? Do they acknowledge that basing their discussions on "ranked wins" is insane, considering how flawed their rankings are? Or that margin of victory in the SEC is a nonsensical "standard" that begs the question? THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! None of this is to pick on Alabama. The Tide aren't doing this themselves, they're a very good team that at this point clearly deserves a spot in the CFB Playoff. The issue is that their treatment by the committee exemplifies the ridiculous double standards being employed here, in order to engineer their preferred outcomes. One of the most aggrieved parties is Tennessee, who beat the Tide on the field, has a similar resume and identical win-loss record, yet sits well behind the Tide. Funnily enough, with all the hand-wringing over Indiana's supposedly "easy" schedule, per ESPN's SP+ metric, which has a "strength of schedule" and "strength of resume" component, Indiana's slate is the 38th toughest in the country? The Georgia Bulldogs? Just 44th. USC's played a harder schedule than Tennessee, yet is buried with little hope of reaching the playoff, even should they beat a top-10 UCLA team on Saturday. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER Then there's Wake Forest, who have obliterated most of the teams on their 56th ranked schedule. Their "resume SP+" ranking is No. 5. They won't be anywhere close to that in Tuesday's poll, because they have the wrong brand name and conference affiliation patch. Will they take it? Well, we'll find out, but based on their track record, it's a near-certainty the answer will be a resounding no.

articles.title: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
articles.body:
Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after reports that Russia was preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.

Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media outlets. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.

Asked about the reports, Rutte said: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hadn't seen the latest reports but dismissed reports citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".

The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".

Rutte told the press conference in Berlin that Nato had a variety of response options.

"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary," he said.

Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, the reports by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites.

Standing alongside Rutte, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".

"Reports that Russia is planning to introduce nuclear weaponry into space are not new, yet they remain no less shocking," he said.

A German government spokesman earlier also did not confirm or deny the reports, but said it was taking the reports "very seriously", AFP reported. The spokesman, however, warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".

Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, said having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario", German paper Handelsblatt reported.

Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit. Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.

In 2024 the US claimed Russia was developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation .

"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.

In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

articles.title: US probes Iran, Russia link after 50 vessels face cyberattack: Report
articles.summary: Washington is looking into whether Iran played a part in dozens of cyberattacks on energy tankers, amid fears that Tehran could be widening the conflict
articles.body: Washington is looking into whether Iran played a part in dozens of cyberattacks on energy tankers, amid fears that Tehran could be widening the conflict beyond the Middle East through cyber operations and plots against Americans.The Wall Street Journal reported on Monday, citing US officials and others familiar with the matter, that up to 50 vessels carrying oil, liquefied petroleum gas, chemicals and other potentially explosive cargoes are believed to have been targeted. According to the report, several ships also received warnings and bomb threats saying they could be blown up.The Journal said Iran is a leading suspect, though US authorities also see Russia as a possible perpetrator. The probe comes as officials in Washington worry the conflict could spill beyond the region through cyber operations and threats against Americans.In a separate development, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Monday that three oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz. It claimed the ships were under US military escort, which it said failed to prevent the incidents.Iranian state news agency IRNA quoted the IRGC as saying the tankers were hit by explosions and fires after striking the mines in the preceding hours. The force cautioned shipping firms and vessel operators against taking unauthorised routes or ignoring maritime warnings, stressing that US military escorts would not excuse them from following the rules and instructions of its Navy's Traffic Control Centre.The IRGC added that vessels using unauthorised routes could be regarded as breaching maritime rules and cooperating with what it termed aggressor forces, and would face action under its announced regulations.You use AI every day.
